name: Cider Braised Short Ribs with Caramelized Onions
why: It's October and apple cider season — this braise is the ultimate cold-weather showstopper: seared beef short ribs cooked low and slow for 3 hours in apple cider, white wine and deeply caramelized onions. It's the kind of hands-off oven cooking you love (moussaka energy) that turns into a restaurant-grade dinner, and the caramelized onions take the bite out of the raw onion flavour completely.
author: Henry
ingredients: 5 lb (2.3 kg) bone-in beef short ribs
2 cups (480 ml) chicken broth or dry white wine
Creamy mashed potatoes, to serve (optional but recommended)

steps: Season the short ribs generously with salt and pepper, then rub with the flour to coat evenly.
Heat a large oven-safe Dutch oven over high heat. Sear the ribs on both sides until deeply browned — about 2-3 minutes per side. Remove to a plate and wipe the pot clean of any grease.
Add the butter and sliced onions, and cook for 5 minutes until softened.
Add ½ cup of the apple cider, season with salt and pepper, and cook for another 5-8 minutes until the cider has evaporated and the onions are a light golden colour.
Stir in the fresh thyme, then nestle the short ribs back into the pot.
Add the remaining 1½ cups apple cider, the chicken broth (or white wine), chopped carrots, smashed garlic and bay leaves. Arrange the apple wedges around the meat.

Cover the pot and roast in the oven for 2½ to 3 hours, until the short ribs are tender and falling off the bone. Check once or twice to make sure the ribs are still about a third submerged in liquid — add a splash of water or cider if needed.
Remove the bay leaves. Ladle the pan sauce and caramelized onions into a large serving bowl, then spoon the ribs on top with a fork.
Serve over a bed of creamy mashed potatoes, drizzled with the pan sauce and onions.

pro_tips: The flour rub on the ribs before searing isn't just for browning — it's a secret thickener that gives the pan sauce its body without any cornflour sludge. Don't skip it.

The whole trick is the caramelized onions: cooking them down slowly with a splash of cider takes the sharp raw bite out and turns them into sweet, jammy strands. Use a dry white wine instead of broth if you want a brighter, more elegant flavour — the cider does the heavy lifting either way.
